input:
A continuous stirred-tank reactor, or CSTR, carries out a neutralisation reaction that is first order with respect to the limiting reactant, meaning that the rate is directly proportional to the concentration of that reactant. The rate constant at the operating temperature is 0.239 min-1, and the mean residence time is 81 min, the mean residence time being the average time a portion of feed spends inside the vessel, obtained by dividing the reactor volume by the volumetric flow rate through it.

For an ideal CSTR at steady state, the conversion achieved is governed by the product of the rate constant and the mean residence time. Multiplying the two together gives 19.359, a dimensionless quantity that compares the time available for reaction with the characteristic time the reaction requires. Because this product is considerably larger than unity, only a small proportion of the limiting reactant passes through the reactor without reacting. Dividing this product by one plus itself, as the steady-state relationship for an ideal CSTR requires, gives a conversion of 95.1%.

The result can be checked against the expected limiting behaviour. If the residence time were zero, no conversion at all would be achieved, while if the product of rate constant and residence time were to grow without limit, the conversion would approach completeness, and the value obtained here sits close to the complete end of that spectrum, as a product of this magnitude would lead one to anticipate. The estimate rests on two assumptions: perfect mixing throughout the vessel, so that the composition everywhere is the same as at the outlet, and constant density, so that the residence time is the same for every portion of feed. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not in fact been carried out, so the perfect-mixing assumption remains unverified for the vessel in question, and the figure should properly be regarded as the ideal-CSTR value corresponding to the stated rate constant and residence time.

A continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant, and the steady-state conversion of that reactant is 95.1%. First order in the limiting reactant means the rate is proportional to that reactant's concentration; the rate constant is 0.239 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time is 81 min. Mean residence time is the reactor volume divided by the volumetric flow through it, and it fixes how long a portion of feed spends in the vessel on average.

For an ideal CSTR at steady state, conversion is set by the product of rate constant and residence time. That product is 19.359, a dimensionless group that compares the time available for reaction with the time the reaction needs: a product well above unity leaves only a small share of the limiting reactant unconverted. Division of the product by one plus the product gives the conversion, and the value obtained is the stated one.

The check on the result is the limiting behaviour. A residence time of zero would give no conversion, and a product growing without bound would drive conversion toward completeness; the stated conversion sits close to the complete end of that range, as a product of this size requires. The estimate assumes perfect mixing, so every part of the vessel holds the same composition as the outlet, and it assumes constant density, so the residence time is the same for every portion of feed. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, so the perfect-mixing assumption is unverified for the vessel in question, and the conversion stands as the ideal-CSTR value at the stated rate constant and residence time.
